results.title: ECB & Climate Risk Management
results.content:
Title: ECB & Climate Risk Management
# The European Central Bank's Approach to Climate Risk Management. Climate and environmental risks are prompting central banks to require their integration into financial institutions' risk management strategies for financial stability. The ECB has developed specific climate risk guidelines and disclosure requirements. These guidelines are part of the broader ECB climate risk management strategy, ensuring that climate risk in the banking sector is adequately addressed and integrated into banks' risk management frameworks. To safeguard the stability of the financial system, the European Central Bank (ECB) has set climate risk guidance to help banks and financial institutions assess the risks climate change poses to their business. The European Central Bank Guide on climate-related and environmental risks outlines how the ECB expects its supervised banks to manage and disclose C&E (climate-related and environmental) risks under current prudential rules. The guide aims to enhance banks' awareness of and preparedness for managing climate-related and environmental risks. Nevertheless, with the mandate that climate and environmental (C&E) risks be fully incorporated into the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) by the end of 2024, and the inclusion of climate-related findings in the 2022 Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP), it can be argued that climate risks have an **indirect** influence on banks' capital requirements. Expectation 8 of the ECB Guide on climate-related and environmental risks relates to **credit risk**, stating that financial institutions must factor in climate and environmental risks when allocating credit, as well as supervise and manage these risks in their loan portfolios, credit process, risk classification and collateral valuations. For example, for physical risks in the financial services industry, you should aim for forward-looking, quantitative, up-to-date climate risk data that enables you to assess your portfolio, identify materiality exposures and report meaningful information and key metrics. In essence, financial institutions should assess the materiality of their climate risks, as well as consider climate-related and environmental risks when creating and executing their business strategy, governance, and risk management structure. Spectra models physical climate risk at the asset level, enabling banks to assess exposure, simulate financial impacts, and produce outputs aligned with ECB stress testing and climate risk disclosure requirements. Spectra supports multiple climate scenarios—including those aligned with NGFS and ECB guidance—allowing banks to test performance across different transition and physical risk pathways.

results.title: ECB climate factor 2026: New risk discount changes refinancing operations - Banking.Vision
results.content: # ECB climate factor 2026: New risk discount changes refinancing operations. This indicates that banks should now prepare their collateral pools for climate change, adjust data and valuation models, and plan early diversification toward lower-emission securities. ECB climate factor 2026: New risk discount changes refinancing operations. ## Focus on climate risks: New ECB climate factor changes refinancing operations. In future, the climate factor will act as an additional risk discount on collateral and thus protect the ECB from potential losses in value. Assets with a high climate risk will be subject to higher discounts in future, which will reduce the lending values and less central bank liquidity can be mobilized. In the remaining preparation time, banks should analyse their collateral pools in detail according to climate risks and establish a classification by issuer, sector and remaining term at an early stage and derive corresponding effects.

results.title: ECB to incorporate climate in corporate bond purchases, collateral framework, disclosure requirements and risk management – Finadium
results.content:
Title: ECB to incorporate climate in corporate bond purchases, collateral framework, disclosure requirements and risk management – Finadium
# ECB to incorporate climate in corporate bond purchases, collateral framework, disclosure requirements and risk management. ### **ECB takes further steps to incorporate climate change into its monetary policy operations**. The Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) has decided to take further steps to include climate change considerations in the Eurosystem’s monetary policy framework. It decided to adjust corporate bond holdings in the Eurosystem’s monetary policy portfolios and its collateral framework, to introduce climate-related disclosure requirements and to enhance its risk management practices. They aim to better take into account climate-related financial risk in the Eurosystem balance sheet and, with reference to our secondary objective, support the green transition of the economy in line with the EU’s climate neutrality objectives. “Within our mandate, we are taking further concrete steps to incorporate climate change into our monetary policy operations. It will assess their effects and adapt them, if necessary: (1) to confirm that they continue to fulfil their monetary policy objectives; (2) to ensure – within its mandate – that the relevant measures continue to support the decarbonisation path to reach the goals of the Paris Agreement and the EU climate neutrality objectives; (3) to respond to future improvements in climate data and climate risk modelling or changes in regulation; and (4) to address additional environmental challenges, within its price stability mandate. Companies and governments need to do their part to address climate risks by enhancing disclosures and following up on their commitments to reduce carbon emissions. The ECB’s work is progressing as outlined in the climate roadmap, and may have to be aligned if and when the timetable in EU legislation changes. The ECB is also including climate change considerations in areas of its work besides monetary policy, including banking supervision, financial stability, economic analysis, statistical data and corporate sustainability. With this commitment, we aim to make a real difference in three ways: (1) by managing and mitigating the financial risk of climate change and assessing its economic impact, (2) by promoting sustainable finance to support an orderly transition towards a low-carbon economy and (3) by sharing our expertise to help foster wider changes in economic behaviour.
